title: Multiwire Branch Circuits & Shared Neutrals

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Shop training area: an isolated 120/208 V MWBC training board behind a clear barrier, three circuits with lamps of different wattages. Matthew beside it. Medium shot.
scenes.on_screen: Job Mindset: Working on a shared neutral
scenes.says: The hazard on a multiwire circuit is the neutral you think is dead. So before the job, identify the whole circuit from the panel schedule, handle ties and grouped conductors. Plan to lock out every breaker that shares that neutral, with enough locks and tags for each. Bring a meter for line-to-line checks and a clamp for neutral current. Turning off your breaker is not enough.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Graphic of a panel with two or three hots and one shared neutral leaving together.
scenes.on_screen: MWBC: 2 or 3 hots on different phases + 1 shared neutral
scenes.says: A multiwire branch circuit is two or more hots with voltage between them, sharing one neutral. Lighting uses them constantly because one neutral can serve two or three circuits. On 120/240, the neutral carries the difference: 10 amps and 7 amps leaves 3 on the neutral. On three-phase with balanced linear loads, it's near zero. With LED drivers, triplen harmonics still add up in the neutral.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech clamps each hot and the neutral on the training board, balanced then unbalanced; readings shown on screen. Presenter voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Same-phase test: measure between the hots. Near 0 V = same phase.
scenes.says: Now the same-phase fault. If two hots get landed on the same phase, the neutral carries the sum. Two 16 amp circuits put 32 amps on a 12 AWG neutral that no breaker protects. It's common after panel work or retrofits. Test it: measure voltage between the hots. You should see 208, 240 or 480. Near zero means same phase. Clamp the neutral to confirm.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Isolated training board behind the barrier: the neutral is opened by a switch built into the board; lamps on one circuit go dim, another goes very bright. Wide shot, no one near the board.
scenes.on_screen: Open neutral: loads in series across line-to-line voltage
scenes.says: Here's an open neutral, on an isolated training board only, behind a barrier. The loads end up in series across line-to-line voltage. The lighter load gets more than its rated voltage, sometimes close to the full 208. The heavier one gets less. That's why you see some lights blazing or failing and others dim. And the neutral downstream of the break can be at dangerous voltage.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Real lighting panel, de-energized and locked out: close-up of a handle-tied pair of breakers and a bundle of hots with their neutral cable-tied together.
scenes.on_screen: 210.4(B) simultaneous disconnect - 210.4(D) grouping - 300.13(B) pigtail neutrals - 410.130(G) luminaire disconnects
scenes.says: The NEC rules, 2023 edition, with your adopted edition governing. 210.4(B): every MWBC needs a way to disconnect all hots at once, a multi-pole breaker or identified handle ties. 210.4(D): group the hots and neutral in the panel. 300.13(B): pigtail neutrals so pulling a device doesn't open the neutral. 410.130(G): luminaire disconnects on MWBCs break all supply conductors, including the neutral.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech at the real panel locks and tags each handle-tied breaker, then tests the meter, checks every conductor including the neutral, and retests the meter. Presenter voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: 1 Identify whole MWBC  2 PPE  3 Measure  4 De-energize ALL + lock each  5 Verify every conductor incl. neutral  6 Repair  7 Re-energize and verify each circuit
scenes.says: Troubleshooting. Identify the whole MWBC. Risk assessment and PPE for energized readings. Measure line-to-line and current on each hot and the neutral, and record them. De-energize every circuit, lock and tag each one. Verify absence of voltage on every conductor, including the neutral, live-dead-live. Repair. Then re-energize and verify voltage at loads on every circuit and recheck neutral current.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew in front of the real panel, medium close-up. Safety callout.
scenes.on_screen: Never open a shared neutral while any circuit on the MWBC is energized.
scenes.says: Never open, disconnect or cut a shared neutral while any circuit on it is energized. It may be carrying the other circuits' current, and opening it puts you in series with the load at up to full circuit voltage. Lock out every circuit that shares the neutral and verify it's dead. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: The open-neutral demonstration (scene 4) must be performed ONLY on an isolated, purpose-built training board behind a barrier, with the neutral opened by a switch built into the board; no person within reach while it is open. Do not depict opening a neutral in a real panel. Real-panel shots in scenes 5-6 are de-energized under LOTO. Demo performer: qualified senior technician.
